transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A new community college program in Ohio is gaining national attention for its innovative approach to helping displaced workers transition into high-demand technology careers. The program, called TechLaunch, offers free six-month training programs in fields such as cybersecurity, cloud computing, and software development, specifically targeted at workers who lost their jobs in declining industries including manufacturing and retail. What makes the program unusual is that it guarantees graduates a job interview with one of more than 50 partner companies, and students receive a living stipend during their training so they don't have to work while studying. In its first two years of operation, TechLaunch has graduated over 400 students, with an 85 percent job placement rate and an average starting salary of 52,000 dollars per year. The program's success has led three other states to announce plans to launch similar initiatives, using a combination of state funding, federal workforce development grants, and corporate sponsorships to cover costs.

2. What makes the program unusual?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: Archaeologists working in Egypt have discovered an ancient cemetery containing more than 1,000 wooden statues and well-preserved mummies dating back approximately 3,500 years to the New Kingdom period. The site, located near the city of Luxor in southern Egypt, includes dozens of elaborately decorated tombs belonging to high-ranking officials and priests, as well as simpler burials for artisans and workers. Among the most remarkable finds is a fully intact tomb belonging to a royal scribe named Djehuty-em-hat, which contains colorful wall paintings depicting scenes from daily life, religious rituals, and the journey to the afterlife. Archaeologists also discovered a cache of 40 sarcophagi in excellent condition, many still containing mummies with their funerary masks and burial goods intact. The Egyptian government hopes the discovery will help revitalize the country's tourism industry, which was severely affected by political unrest and the COVID-19 pandemic. Plans are already underway to open parts of the site to the public within the next year.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: A major European car manufacturer has announced that it will stop producing vehicles with internal combustion engines by 2035, becoming one of the first traditional automakers to commit to a complete transition to electric vehicles. The company says it will invest more than 80 billion dollars over the next decade in electric vehicle development, battery manufacturing, and charging infrastructure. Under the plan, the company will launch 25 new electric models by 2030, with the goal of electric vehicles making up 100 percent of its new car sales in Europe by 2035 and globally by 2040. Industry analysts say the announcement represents a significant milestone in the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, putting pressure on other major car manufacturers to accelerate their own electric vehicle plans. The company also announced partnerships with several renewable energy companies to ensure that its manufacturing facilities and the electricity used to charge its vehicles come from 100 percent renewable sources by the same deadline.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Man (Ethan): Hey, Sophia. Did you watch that documentary about plastic pollution last night? It was really eye-opening, but also kind of depressing.

Woman (Sophia): I watched about half of it, Ethan, but then I had to stop because I was getting too upset. It's horrifying to see how much plastic is ending up in the ocean and in our food. I feel like I should be doing more, but I don't even know where to start.

Man: I know what you mean. That's how I felt too. But actually, the documentary ended on a somewhat positive note—there are things individuals can do, and policy changes are happening. One of the things they suggested was starting with reducing single-use plastics in our daily lives.

Woman: Like bringing reusable bags to the store? I already do that. And I have a reusable water bottle. But I still feel like I throw away so much plastic—food packaging especially seems impossible to avoid.

Man: That's true. But they pointed out that even small changes add up. They suggested shopping at bulk stores where you can bring your own containers, and choosing products with less packaging. Also, I didn't realize that synthetic clothing like polyester releases microplastics every time you wash it. You can buy special filters for your washing machine to catch those.
Woman: I had no idea about the clothing! That's crazy. But buying all new containers and special washing machine filters sounds expensive. Is this only something wealthy people can do?

Man: The documentary addressed that too. Some changes don't cost anything at all—like refusing plastic straws and cutlery when you order takeout, making things last longer instead of replacing them, buying secondhand. And many cities are starting to implement better recycling programs and bans on certain single-use plastics.

Woman: That's good to hear. I feel like individual actions are important, but it seems like the biggest changes have to come from governments and corporations. I can't believe how much unnecessary packaging companies use for everything.

Man: Exactly. But they said that consumer pressure is what drives companies to change. If more people refuse to buy over-packaged products and demand alternatives, businesses will adapt. There's also a growing movement to hold producers responsible for the entire lifecycle of their packaging, not just expect consumers to deal with the waste.

Woman: Maybe we should start a recycling and sustainability club on campus? I know there are a lot of students who care about this issue, but there isn't really an organized group doing anything about it.

Man: That's a fantastic idea! We could organize documentary screenings, do campus clean-up days, and maybe even work with the university administration to reduce plastic use in the cafeteria and campus stores. I'd definitely join.
Woman: Let's do it. I'll talk to the student activities office about how to register a new club, and you can ask some of our friends if they'd be interested in helping organize the first meeting.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
8. What were Ethan and Sophia discussing?
9. Why did Sophia stop watching the documentary?
10. What microplastic source did Sophia learn about?
11. What do they decide to do?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Tom): Good morning, everybody. Thanks for coming to this meeting of the university events committee. We're here today to start planning this year's spring festival, which will be held on Saturday, April 26th. First, let's hear from Emma about what worked and what didn't work at last year's event.

Woman (Emma): Thanks, Tom. Overall last year's festival was a big success—we had record attendance, and the feedback surveys were mostly positive. But there were a few issues. The food vendors ran out of food by 3 PM because we had more people than expected, the live music started late because of sound system problems, and the lines for the carnival games were really long in the afternoon.

Man: Good points. So this year we need more food vendors, better sound equipment, and more activities so people don't have to wait in lines. Let's talk about the budget first. The student association has allocated 15,000 pounds for this year's festival—same as last year. Does anyone have ideas for new attractions we could add?

Woman: I was thinking we could add a petting zoo with farm animals—kids from the local primary school always come, and they love that kind of thing. Also, maybe a craft fair where students and local artisans can sell their handmade goods. We could charge a small fee for booths, which would help cover costs.
Man: A petting zoo would cost money to rent, but the craft fair could actually bring in revenue. That's smart. What about food? We had eight vendors last year. How many should we aim for this year?

Woman: At least twelve, I think. And we should ask them to bring 30 percent more food than they think they'll need. I also think we should have more diverse food options—last year it was almost all burgers and pizza, and some students mentioned wanting vegetarian and international food options.

Man: Agreed. Now, about music—last year we had three student bands playing. Should we do the same this year, or do we want to try to get a bigger act? We have about 3,000 pounds in the budget allocated for entertainment.

Woman: A professional band would be nice, but student bands are much cheaper and they appreciate the exposure. I say stick with student performers—maybe add a couple more acts, and make sure we have a professional sound company this time to avoid technical problems. We could also have an open mic session between sets to showcase more talent.
Man: That makes sense. Let's also think about volunteers—we need about 40 people to help set up, run activities, and clean up afterward. We can offer free food and T-shirts as incentives.

Woman: I can coordinate volunteer sign-ups. We should also make sure we have a rain plan this year. There were thunderstorms predicted for last year's date, and we had no backup plan. If it rains, we'd need to move everything indoors to the gymnasium and student union.

Man: Excellent point. I'll talk to facilities management about reserving indoor spaces as a backup. Let's split up responsibilities—Emma, you can handle vendors and entertainment. I'll work on budget, permits, and the rain plan. Everyone else, please reach out to student organizations and spread the word about volunteering. Our next meeting is in two weeks.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: Effective time management is one of the most important skills for academic and professional success, yet it is something that many people struggle with throughout their lives. The good news is that time management is not an innate talent that some people are born with—it is a set of habits and strategies that can be learned and practiced by anyone.

One of the most common time management mistakes people make is failing to prioritize tasks. Not all tasks are equally important, yet many people treat them as if they are, spending their days reacting to urgent but unimportant requests instead of focusing on activities that will help them reach their long-term goals. The Eisenhower Matrix, a decision-making tool attributed to former U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, helps solve this problem by dividing tasks into four categories: urgent and important (do immediately), important but not urgent (schedule for later), urgent but not important (delegate if possible), and neither urgent nor important (eliminate entirely).

Another common trap is multitasking—trying to do several things at once. Despite the common belief that some people are good at multitasking, research consistently shows that multitasking reduces productivity and increases errors. What people think of as multitasking is actually rapid task-switching, which costs time and mental energy as the brain shifts attention back and forth between activities. You can accomplish more and produce higher-quality work by focusing on one task at a time, giving it your full attention, and then moving on to the next task.

Procrastination is perhaps the biggest time management challenge for most people, especially students. Research has found that procrastination is rarely caused by laziness—it is usually a response to feeling overwhelmed, anxious about doing a task perfectly, or simply not knowing where to start. Strategies for overcoming procrastination include breaking large projects into small, manageable steps, working for just 25 minutes at a time (known as the Pomodoro Technique), removing distractions from your workspace, and rewarding yourself after completing difficult tasks. Perhaps the most powerful antidote to procrastination is simply getting started—once you begin a task, it often becomes less intimidating, and momentum carries you forward.

Finally, effective time management includes scheduling downtime. Many people think productivity means filling every minute of the day with activity, but research shows that taking regular breaks and getting enough rest actually improves productivity, creativity, and decision-making. The human brain cannot maintain high levels of focus indefinitely; it needs periods of rest to consolidate learning, process information, and recharge mental energy.

16. What is the Eisenhower Matrix?
17. What does research say about multitasking?
18. What is one strategy for overcoming procrastination?

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: The British seaside holiday has a long and beloved history that stretches back nearly 200 years. Before the 1840s, going to the seaside for pleasure was largely an activity for the wealthy upper classes, who would visit spa towns and coastal resorts for their health, believing that sea air and bathing in seawater had medicinal properties. The Industrial Revolution changed everything, as the growth of railways made it possible for factory workers and their families to travel to the coast cheaply and quickly for day trips or week-long holidays during their annual time off.

By the late 19th century, seaside towns such as Blackpool, Brighton, and Bournemouth had boomed, building piers, promenades, amusement arcades, and grand hotels to accommodate the millions of working-class holidaymakers arriving by train each summer. The classic British seaside experience included building sandcastles, riding donkeys on the beach, eating fish and chips wrapped in newspaper, watching Punch and Judy shows, and attending variety performances in end-of-the-pier theaters. The introduction of paid holiday leave in the 20th century, particularly the Holidays with Pay Act of 1938, meant that even more working families could afford a week or two at the seaside.

The 1960s and 1970s saw the beginning of decline for many traditional British seaside resorts, as affordable package holidays abroad made it possible for ordinary people to travel to Spain, France, and other Mediterranean destinations in search of reliable sunshine and warmer weather. Many seaside towns fell into economic decline, with hotels closing, piers falling into disrepair, and amusement arcades being replaced by cheap souvenir shops and gambling establishments.

In recent years, however, there has been something of a revival. Many British people are rediscovering the charms of domestic holidays—often called "staycations"—driven in part by economic uncertainty, environmental concerns about air travel, and nostalgia for simpler holidays. Seaside towns are undergoing regeneration, with old piers being restored, independent shops and cafes opening, and new attractions drawing visitors year-round rather than just during the summer. While cheap foreign package holidays haven't disappeared, the British seaside holiday has proven that it still holds a special place in the nation's heart.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Public libraries are among the most beloved and widely used public institutions in the United States, with nearly 80 percent of adults saying they have used a public library at some point in their lives, and over half reporting that they have used one in the past year. Yet the role of libraries has changed dramatically over the past two decades, transforming them from quiet buildings primarily filled with books into dynamic community hubs offering a wide range of free services and resources.

The most obvious change is in technology access. As internet access has become essential for education, employment, and accessing government services, libraries have stepped in to bridge the digital divide. Virtually all public libraries in the U.S. offer free public Wi-Fi and public computers for patrons to use. For many low-income families, elderly patrons, and people experiencing homelessness, the library is their only reliable access to high-speed internet. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many libraries even expanded Wi-Fi access to their parking lots so people could use the internet when buildings were closed.

Beyond technology, libraries have expanded their offerings to meet community needs. Many libraries now offer free literacy programs, English language classes for immigrants, job search assistance, tax preparation help, and after-school programs for children and teenagers. Some have added maker spaces with 3D printers, recording studios, and tools that people can use for entrepreneurship or creative projects. Others loan out much more than books—instruments, tools, museum passes, seeds for gardening, and even cooking equipment are available at some libraries.

Contrary to predictions that the internet would make libraries obsolete, library usage remains high. What has changed is what people use libraries for. While books remain central—circulation of physical and digital books continues to grow—people increasingly come to libraries for human connection, help navigating complex systems, and free access to resources they cannot afford on their own. Librarians have evolved too, serving as information specialists who help people find reliable health information, apply for jobs, navigate government websites, and distinguish credible news sources from misinformation.

Despite their popularity and importance, public libraries face ongoing challenges including budget pressures, political debates about what books should be on shelves, and the need to adapt to changing community needs. Yet surveys consistently show that libraries are among the most trusted institutions in American society, and communities consistently vote to fund them through taxes, recognizing that public libraries provide enormous value and opportunity for people of all ages and backgrounds.

23. What percentage of American adults have used a public library?
24. What important role do libraries play in bridging the digital divide?
25. According to the passage, how have librarians' roles evolved?
